_readme.purpose: Single source of truth for what each sprite action IS. Two pipelines read it: the ControlNet img2img path (tasks.generate_spritesheet_task) reads `match`/`prompt`/`strength`/`ip_adapter_scale`/`view`, and the 2D Qwen-Image-Edit conveyor (build-sheet.py, the one the UI drives) reads `sheet_id`/`sheet_label`/`frames`. Edit this file to change how an action looks or animates; no code change is needed.
_readme.reload: Re-read automatically when this file's mtime changes, so edits take effect on the next sheet WITHOUT restarting the sprite_worker container. Malformed JSON is logged and the previous good version stays loaded.
_readme.matching: actions[] is ORDERED and matched in order. An action name from the UI is lowercased, then the first entry with any of its `match` substrings contained in that name wins. Specific entries must come before general ones: 'move right' has to win before a bare 'move' would.
_readme.fallback: An action matching nothing is sent to the model as its own raw text, so a hand-typed custom action still works.
_readme.diagonals: Diagonals ALIAS onto the horizontal cardinal: up-right and down-right render as move_right, up-left and down-left as move_left. That is a 4-way conveyor serving 8-way input, which is what a large share of 2D games ship - a side-facing sprite reads correctly while moving diagonally, where a front or back sprite does not. It costs nothing: no extra generation, no extra view core, and left/right are already mirror-consistent. WHY IT MATTERS: matching is contiguous-substring and ORDERED, and 'move up right' CONTAINS 'move up'. Before these keys existed every diagonal silently resolved to the BACK view and discarded the horizontal component entirely - measured, 'move up right' rendered as 'back view, facing away'. It failed silently, which is worse than failing. The horizontal entries sit before the vertical ones in actions[], so their diagonal keys win by position; do not reorder actions[] without re-running scripts/validate-actions.py.

what_to_write.rule: ControlNet supplies a skeleton that already fixes where every limb is, far more precisely than words can. Prompt text that argues with the skeleton makes both signals worse. So do NOT describe limb positions here.
do_describe: FACING - which way the camera sees the character. The skeleton encodes this too, so words reinforce it rather than fight it.
INTENT and energy - 'aggressive', 'off balance', 'at rest'. Mood is not a joint position.
EFFECTS - fire, smoke, embers, impact. A skeleton cannot ask for flames; only the prompt can.
do_not_describe: Which leg is forward, arm angles, stride length - the skeleton owns all of it.
Art style, background, or the character's own identity - those come from the core image's prompt, which is appended after this text.

token_budget.why: CLIP keeps 77 tokens and silently discards the rest - a clause past the cut is absent from every generation while still looking present in this file.
token_budget.shared_with: This prompt is only the FIRST part of what the model receives. The core image's own prompt and the style suffix share the same 77 tokens.
token_budget.guidance: Keep each `prompt` under about 24 tokens (roughly 18 words). Measured against a 31-token core prompt the full frame prompt lands at 67-72, leaving very little slack - a longer core prompt WILL truncate.
token_budget.how_to_check: check_prompt_length() in tasks.py logs a WARNING naming the action whenever a frame prompt overruns. Watch the worker log after editing; do not assume it fits.

_readme.pose_cycle: Informational only - names the skeleton in poses.py that drives this action's limbs. Changing it here has no effect; edit poses.POSE_LIBRARY instead. Listed so the pose and the words can be checked for agreement (a side-view skeleton with a front-view prompt is the bug this field exists to make visible).

strength.what: OPTIONAL img2img strength for this action only, 0..1. How much of the core image the model may paint over. Omit to use POSED_STRENGTH (0.75) from tasks.py.
strength.tradeoff: Low keeps the character but freezes its appearance. High frees the appearance but drifts toward a different character. There is no value that is right for every action, which is why this is per-action.
strength.when_to_raise: Two cases. (1) The action must ADD something the core does not contain - flames, a bow, a spell. (2) The action must MOVE THE BODY substantially. Case 2 was originally documented as unnecessary, on the theory that ControlNet supplies the pose so strength can stay low. That was measured and it is FALSE: at 0.60 the init image outvotes the skeleton and the legs do not move at all. A walk rendered at 0.60 is a character standing still while a walk skeleton is ignored.
strength.measured: Burning, same prompt, seed and skeleton, fraction of the sprite that is flame-coloured: 0.60 -> 0.07% (no fire at all), 0.75 -> 4.36% (visible flames, character still intact). Below about 0.70 there is not enough denoising freedom left to add fire.
strength.ceiling: Do not exceed ~0.75. At 0.75 with an EMPTY negative prompt the character was lost outright (came back in different clothes), and higher still reintroduces the OpenPose skeleton's own limb colours printing onto the sprite. NEGATIVE_FRAME is what holds identity together up here - do not strip it to chase an effect.
strength.measured_pose: Walk cycle, leg motion at controlnet_conditioning_scale 1.0: strength 0.60 -> legs static, the sprite stands there; 0.75 -> visibly striding, character intact; 0.90 -> striding but the design starts changing; 1.00 -> a different character entirely. Raising controlnet_conditioning_scale instead of strength does NOT substitute - 0.60 with scale 1.6 was still static, because the problem is that too few denoising steps run to move anything, not that the skeleton is too quiet.
strength.measured_quality: Strength is not only about motion and identity - it decides whether the frame is REDRAWN at all. Below ~0.70 the output is the original core lightly modified, so it keeps the core painterly rendering and never becomes crisp pixel art. Idle at 0.60 came back with an unreadable face and a smeared torso; at 0.75 with the IP-Adapter holding identity it is clean. If a row looks mushy rather than wrong, this is the knob.

ip_adapter_scale.what: OPTIONAL 0..1. Re-injects the core image through cross-attention at EVERY denoising step, instead of only as the starting latent the way img2img does. Omit or 0 to leave it off, which is the default everywhere.
ip_adapter_scale.why_it_exists: img2img uses the core exactly once - it noises it to `strength` and denoises from there, after which nothing refers back to the original. That is why `strength` alone decides both how much identity survives and how much freedom the prompt gets. This gives identity its own channel, the same way ControlNet gave pose its own channel.
ip_adapter_scale.cost: Loads a CLIP image encoder that stays resident in VRAM next to the checkpoint (~2.6GB on disk). Only loaded when at least one action in the sheet sets a non-zero scale, and unloaded again when none do.
ip_adapter_scale.critical_warning: DO NOT set this on an action that must ADD something the core image does not contain. The adapter anchors appearance to a reference with no flames, no bow and no spell in it, so it spends every step pulling back toward not-having-them. Measured on burning at strength 0.85, flame coverage: no adapter 15.57%, scale 0.35 -> 0.27%, scale 0.50 and above -> 0.00%. There is no scale that escapes this; it is what the adapter does.
ip_adapter_scale.where_it_helps: Actions that only change POSE, where there is no added effect for it to suppress and identity anchoring is therefore free: the walks, idle, and close melee. Start around 0.4-0.6.
ip_adapter_scale.tuning: Higher means the output clings harder to the core. Too high and every frame converges on the core's own pose and the animation stops moving, because the adapter fights ControlNet as well.

_readme.view: Which way the character FACES: front | back | left | right. Used two ways. (1) On a checkpoint listing this view in tasks.VIEW_TRIGGERS, the matching trained trigger is prepended to the frame prompt - that is how a real back view is obtained rather than a hallucinated one. (2) On a checkpoint without view triggers it falls back to derive_side_core for profile views. Omit for actions with no meaningful facing.

sheet_frames.what: The `frames` block is the CONVEYOR's animation table: an ordered list of poses per view family. actions.py builds its ACTIONS dict from every entry that has one, keyed by `sheet_id`.
sheet_frames.why_here: These poses used to be a hardcoded dict in actions.py while this file sat unread by the conveyor - two action tables, and the UI drove the one you could not edit. Adding an action meant a code change and a worker rebuild.
sheet_frames.reload: Same mtime-cache discipline as the prompts above: edits take effect on the next sheet without restarting sprite_worker, and malformed JSON keeps the last good version loaded.
sheet_frames.families: Keys are view families, not directions: front | back | side. `view_families` below maps the eight compass directions onto them. `side` is REQUIRED and is the fallback for any family an action does not list - correct for genuinely view-independent actions (idle, sway) and a visible but harmless approximation otherwise.
sheet_frames.frame_count: The length of the list IS the maximum frame count for that action. /api/jobs refuses a request for more, and the UI caps its input from /api/action-catalog. Lists of different lengths across families are safe - each renders its own length.
sheet_frames.rule: A frame pose must change the SILHOUETTE as seen from THAT camera. Motion along the view axis does not exist in the output. Profile cameras get sagittal motion (strides, thrusts, lunges); front and back get vertical and lateral motion (knee lifts, overhead swings, arms going wide). Ask a front camera for a forward punch and the model draws the nearest thing it can see - measured, a literal T-pose in six of eight directions.
sheet_frames.write_poses_not_verbs: 'walking' is a process and the model picks the same instant of it every time, so four frames of a walk come back as four frames of standing. Name limb positions instead, so each frame is a different, checkable target.
sheet_frames.effects_stay_on_the_body: An effect must stay ATTACHED to the character. A pose that asks for one to fill the frame - 'energy discharged outward', 'explosion', 'shockwave' - gets one, and it takes the background with it: the model paints a dark full-frame ground behind the light, pixelate.key_background finds no background colour in the corners, and the cell composes as an OPAQUE TILE with the character buried inside it. Measured 2026-08-25 on cast frame 2: 64.1% opaque against ~20% for every other cell in the same sheet, a solid black square in the middle of the row. Name where the effect IS - at the hands, between the palms, at the fingertips - not how far it travels.

_readme.view_families: Which prompt set each compass direction uses. Left and right profiles share one: they are the same view family, mirrored (see domain.md).

actions.label: Move Right
actions._why_diagonals: Diagonals alias onto the horizontal cardinal - see _readme.diagonals. These keys sit in THIS entry rather than their own because move_right is matched before move_up, and 'move up right' contains 'move up'.
actions.prompt: strict side view profile, facing right, walking to the right, full stride, arms swinging, steady forward motion
actions._why_ip_adapter: A/B at strength 0.75 with a stride metric (foot spread per frame): ON [60.5,56.3,59.7,56.4] stride 7.1 and correctly alternating contact/passing; OFF [62.7,63.9,62.0,64.0] stride 3.2. The adapter HELPS the walk - it was expected to fight the stride by anchoring the core standing pose, and it does not.
actions._why_strength: Uses the POSED_STRENGTH default (0.75). At the old 0.60 default the walk skeleton was ignored and the legs stayed planted.

actions.label: Move Left
actions._why_diagonals: Mirror of move_right's diagonal aliasing - see _readme.diagonals.
actions.prompt: strict side view profile, facing left, walking to the left, full stride, arms swinging, steady forward motion
actions._why_ip_adapter: Mirror of move_right; same cycle, same measured benefit.
actions._why_strength: Uses the POSED_STRENGTH default (0.75). At the old 0.60 default the walk skeleton was ignored and the legs stayed planted.

actions.label: Bow (Ranged)
actions._why_strength: Must ADD a bow and arrow the core image does not contain, same additive case as burning. Swept against the bow row: 0.72 rendered an obvious bow but lost the character outright (a green zombie came back as a pale bald human); 0.66 keeps the character at the cost of a fainter weapon.
actions.prompt: firing a wooden bow, arrow nocked and drawn back, archer taking aim at a distant target, taut bowstring
actions._why_ip_adapter: OFF: this action must ADD something absent from the core, which the adapter actively suppresses. See _readme.ip_adapter_scale.critical_warning.
actions._why_view: front, not right: BOW and SLING are authored front-facing in poses.py because what makes a bow or sling legible is the shape the two arms make against each other, and a profile hides one arm behind the other. The view field must match the skeleton geometry; validate-actions.py enforces it.
